currentContext.business: NTPC is among India's largest integrated energy conglomerates, with a presence across the energy value chain and a growing portfolio of conventional and renewable energy assets. The Group generates and sells electricity from coal, gas, hydro, renewable and pumped-storage capacity to distribution utilities and other beneficiaries under a payment-security framework of Letters of Credit and Tri-Partite Agreements, and complements this through subsidiaries and joint ventures engaged in power trading, captive coal mining, nuclear energy, energy efficiency, engineering services and allied businesses. Its captive mining arm NTPC Mining Limited operates coal mines that supply the thermal fleet, and its trading arm NVVN handles power trading, rooftop/ground-mounted solar, waste-to-energy and carbon management.

Power Trading (NVVN): Cross-border power trading (including the Punatsangchu-II hydro project in Bhutan)

currentContext.strengths: Scale: NTPC Group installed capacity of 89.1 GW as on 31 March 2026 (from 79.9 GW), the largest integrated power utility in India, generating 432.2 BU and contributing 23.6% of India's total power generation|Execution: record capacity addition of ~9,618 MW in FY 2025-26 versus ~3,972 MW in FY 2024-25 (+142%), the highest-ever in a single year|Operating efficiency: NTPC coal PLF of 72.0% against national coal PLF of 65.5%, an outperformance of ~6.47 percentage points; NTPC's coal plants continued to significantly outperform the national average|Fuel security: 100% fuel tie-up for thermal capacity through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements with CIL and SCCL, with total Annual Contracted Quantity of 256.92 MMT across the NTPC group|Backward integration into mining: 43.5 MMT of coal sourced from captive mines; captive coal production of 48.65 MMT (6.22% higher YoY), nearly 18% of annual requirement; NTPC Mining Limited is stated to be the third-largest coal mining company in India|Import substitution: NTPC offset the shortfall from linked sources without procuring imported coal, thereby reducing the overall cost of power generation|Pipeline depth: 34.2 GW under construction as on 31 March 2026 (versus 33.6 GW), maintaining a strong capacity pipeline even after record commissioning|Diversification across the energy value chain via 11 subsidiaries, 17 joint ventures (including 2 international) and 9 step-down subsidiaries covering conventional and renewable generation, power trading, mining, nuclear, energy efficiency and engineering services|Capital-markets standing: 33rd consecutive year of dividend declaration in FY 2025-26; a Board-formulated Dividend Distribution Policy under SEBI LODR Regulation 43A|Leadership continuity and sector depth in the executive team (CMD with over 36 years in power and energy; functional directors with 35-37 years' experience each)
currentContext.strategies: Four stated growth priorities: meeting India's rising electricity demand; strengthening energy security through domestic capabilities; expanding clean and flexible energy infrastructure; and leveraging digital technologies to improve efficiency and reliability.|Clean energy transition strategy anchored on a corporate plan targeting 149 GW of total installed capacity by 2032 including 60 GW from renewable energy, with a further aspiration of reaching 244 GW by 2037.|Scale and efficiency in the core: continued focus on scale, efficiency and clean energy expansion to make the business model resilient to changing sector dynamics.|Retain and upgrade the thermal fleet rather than exit it - investments in emission control systems, flexible operations, biomass co-firing, water conservation, ash utilisation and carbon management to make thermal assets more efficient and environmentally responsible.|Fuel self-reliance through captive mining: NTPC Mining Limited operating six mines with three under development, with captive coal production supplying nearly 18% of annual requirement.|Build out storage: expand pumped storage projects and battery energy storage systems, plus investment in next-generation long-duration storage technologies including CO2-based energy storage systems and vanadium redox flow batteries.|Enter and scale nuclear: entry via the Mahi Banswara project in Rajasthan, with studies across 34 sites in 13 States and a site selection report for one location submitted to the Department of Atomic Energy.|Digital-first operations: integrate artificial intelligence, predictive analytics and advanced forecasting across generation, renewable, mining and maintenance operations to improve plant availability, optimise operations, reduce costs and strengthen safety; ICT initiatives during FY26 included Wagon Tippler-Safe Operation, Demand-based Coal Planning and Cost Optimisation, Advanced Pattern Recognition, AI-generated synopses of e-Office files, Automated Summary Sheets and 'Talk to Document - Jyotibot'.|Strengthen enterprise risk management: ERM framework revised in July 2025 to align with ISO 31000:2018, overseen by a Board-level Risk Management Committee; Funding intent is explicit: during FY 2025-26 shareholders passed a special resolution by postal ballot (23 July 2025) authorising the raising of funds up to Rs 18,000 crore through issue of Non-Convertible Debentures / Bonds on a private placement basis. currentContext.expansion: FY 2025-26 was NTPC's largest build year since inception. On a standalone basis the Company added 1,823 MW to reach 60,796 MW as at 31 March 2026 (against 59,413 MW a year earlier), after permanently discontinuing operations of 440 MW at Tanda Stage-I with effect from 1 September 2025. At the Group level 9,618 MW was added - including 7,795 MW by subsidiaries and joint ventures - taking Group installed capacity to 89,108 MW from 79,930 MW; Group commercial capacity rose to 87,977 MW, an addition of 8,488 MW. The long-term Corporate Plan aims for 60 GW of renewable energy capacity and 149 GW of total installed capacity (and 1 GW PSP) by 2032, and 244 GW of total installed capacity (and 6.2 GW of PSP) by 2037, pursued through both organic and inorganic expansion across thermal, hydro, renewable and nuclear. As on 31 March 2026, projects aggregating 34,188 MW were under implementation, of which 20,615 MW sits in subsidiaries and joint ventures; the under-construction portfolio comprises 16,520 MW of coal-based projects (12,520 MW at NTPC, 4,000 MW at subsidiaries/JVs), 2,631 MW of hydro (811 MW at NTPC, 1,820 MW at subsidiaries/JVs) and 15,037 MW of renewable energy (242 MW at NTPC, 14,795 MW at subsidiaries/JVs). In hydro, the Group has 4,475 MW of operational hydropower capacity and is expanding through the 2,631 MW under implementation. In nuclear, the flagship is the Mahi Banswara Rajasthan Atomic Power Project (4 x 700 MW), executed through the strategic vehicle ASHVINI (the NTPC-NPCIL joint venture) with NTPC Parmanu Urja Nigam Limited (NPUNL) as the dedicated nuclear subsidiary; approximately 34 potential sites across multiple states have been identified, with Small Modular Reactors and advanced fuels as emerging technologies and capability development through BARC, NPCIL, IGCAR and international collaborations, aligned to India's 100 GW nuclear vision by 2047. In renewables, commissioned capacity as on 31 March 2026 was 11,547 MW (10,654 MW solar and 893 MW wind), with 15,040 MW under execution (9,403 MW solar and 5,637 MW wind), supported by investments in utility-scale solar, wind, hybrid projects and Ultra Mega Renewable Energy Power Parks. Under National Solar Mission Phase-I, for which NTPC through NVVN was nodal agency, commissioned capacity stood at 733 MW with 4,941 million units of bundled solar power supplied during FY 2025-26. In distributed renewables, 61.72 MW of rooftop solar had been commissioned through NVVN under RESCO and PMC models for Central Ministries, Government Departments and public institutions, with a further 139 MW under implementation and 22.62 MW under tendering. In waste-to-energy, the 600 TPD Varanasi Waste-to-Charcoal project was commissioned during FY 2025-26, producing over 3,000 tonnes of green charcoal supplied to NTPC Unchahar for co-firing; further plants are under implementation at Bhopal (400 TPD), Hubballi-Dharwad (200 TPD), Noida-Greater Noida (900 TPD) and Gorakhpur (500 TPD), development has been initiated at Meerut (900 TPD), and project-management support is being extended to upcoming facilities at Gurugram and Faridabad. Commercially, the Company achieved 100% realisation of bills due for collection under a payment-security framework of Letters of Credit and Tri-Partite Agreements, and sold a record 8,285 MU through power exchanges. Projects are executed through an Integrated Project Management and Control System (IPMCS) covering Engineering Management, Quality Assurance & Inspection, Contract Management and Site Management Control Centres, aimed at timely commissioning within approved cost parameters. NOTE ON AN INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE AR: the Directors' Report states 15,037 MW of renewable projects under implementation while the Group overview section states 15,040 MW under execution (9,403 MW solar + 5,637 MW wind); both are reproduced above as stated and neither has been reconciled or adjusted.
currentContext.mdna: India's electricity demand is projected to grow at 6-6.5% per annum, significantly higher than the global average of approximately 2.8%, driven by rising industrialization, urbanization, digitalization and improving standards of living.|Peak demand crossed 270 GW in FY26 and is projected by CEA to reach about 459 GW by FY36; the National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projects electricity demand of ~3365 BU by FY 2035-36, underscoring continued requirement for substantial capacity additions.|The rapid expansion of AI, cloud computing and data centres will increase demand for reliable, high-quality, round-the-clock power; expansion in manufacturing, infrastructure, electric mobility, urbanisation and digital services is expected to sustain growth.|Renewables are structurally displacing coal: NTPC Group generation was 432.2 BU in FY 2025-26, marginally lower than 438.6 BU in FY 2024-25, primarily reflecting the national trend of RE displacing coal generation during solar-rich periods and a stronger early monsoon reducing thermal dispatch.|India's thermal generation declined about 4% and coal-based generation about 3.7% in FY 2025-26, while RE generation (including hydro) grew ~18%, led by solar (~20%) and wind (~27%); gas-based generation declined ~18%.|Storage economics are inflecting: global battery pack costs dropped 45% Y-o-Y to nearly $70/kWh in 2025, reducing levelized cost of storage and driving capacity additions; CEA expects India to add ~174 GW / 888 GWh of storage capacity by 2035.|Counterparty health is improving: the DISCOM ACS-ARR gap narrowed to Rs 0.06/kWh in FY 2024-25 from Rs 0.21/kWh in FY 2023-24, AT&C losses fell to 15.04%, and legacy dues declined from Rs 1,39,947 crore in 2022 to Rs 3,330 crore by March 2026 under the amended Late Payment Surcharge Rules.|Regulatory tailwinds for storage and nuclear: CERC Tariff Regulations (Second Amendment) 2026 created a framework for Energy Storage Systems co-located with thermal plants and ISTS with defined norms (battery life 15 years, RoE 14%, availability 90%, efficiency >=85%); the SHANTI Act, 2025 permits private and foreign participation (up to 49% FDI) in nuclear; customs duty exemption on nuclear project imports extended until 2035.|Demand-side mandates: the Renewable Consumption Obligation raises renewable consumption targets from ~30% in FY 2024-25 to ~43% by FY 2029-30 for DISCOMs, open access consumers and captive users, while RGO compliance has been made voluntary for thermal stations commissioned after April 2025, giving greater flexibility in renewable capacity planning.|Thermal flexibility economics: the CERC Order of October 2025 allows thermal generating units to undertake unit shutdown when scheduled below 50% of capacity, improving operational efficiency.|Cost tailwind for renewables build-out: GST on renewable equipment reduced from 12% to 5%, with REEIMS launched and incentives for domestic battery manufacturing.|Long-run sector investment thesis: NITI Aayog's February 2026 report projects electricity at nearly 60% of total energy consumption by 2070, non-fossil at about 98% of power generation, and cumulative power-sector investment of approximately USD 14.2 trillion through 2070.|With around 35 GW of projects under construction, NTPC has a strong growth pipeline for the coming years (Chairman & Managing Director's letter).|Under Construction capacity of 34.2 GW as on 31 March 2026 versus 33.6 GW a year earlier - 'Maintaining strong capacity pipeline even after record capacity commissioning' (MD&A segment-wise performance table).|NTPC is a power utility and does not disclose a conventional order book; the pipeline above is the capacity-under-construction disclosure and is the closest equivalent stated in the routed text.

risks.risk: Thermal utilisation structurally eroding as renewables displace coal
risks.note: Stated as a Weakness in the MD&A SWOT: 'The increasing penetration of renewable energy has led to a decline in coal PLF (down by ~5 percentage points), impacting utilisation levels of thermal assets.' The SWOT bullet quantifies it as 'Coal PLF declining (-5.41 ppts) due to RE displacement'. This matters because the thermal fleet remains the bulk of NTPC's earning asset base and PLF drives fixed-cost recovery and incentive economics.

'Gas-based capacity continues to remain underutilised, primarily due to fuel availability and pricing constraints.' A structural stranded-asset risk rather than a cyclical one, since it is driven by fuel supply and price rather than demand.

risks.risk: Duck curve - daytime solar surplus with steep evening ramps
risks.note: 'The increasing share of renewable energy (RE) introduces operational challenges, including the duck curve effect, characterised by periods of surplus solar generation and steep ramping requirements for thermal capacities.' Management notes the rate of increase in peak demand may surpass the rate of growth of energy demand, leading to sharper peaks from cooling load, data centre and EV demand 'which maybe difficult for coal plants to serve effectively'. Partial mitigation is stated: CERC tariff regulations offer a higher percentage of RoE for higher ramp-rate capability, and CEA's National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projects thermal capacity up to 315 GW by 2035-36, indicating continued need for coal-based reliability, ramping and reserve peaking.

risks.risk: Grid integration complexity as variable RE penetration rises
risks.note: 'Higher penetration of variable RE increases grid integration complexity, requiring enhanced flexibility, storage solutions, and system balancing capabilities.' Listed as a Threat in the SWOT matrix.

Listed as a Threat: 'Transmission bottlenecks in RE-rich states (Rajasthan, Gujarat)'. A direct evacuation constraint on NTPC's own large solar and wind build-out, which is concentrated in exactly those geographies.

risks.risk: Falling BESS tariffs making solar-plus-storage competitive against new thermal capacity
risks.note: 'a downward trend in the BESS tariffs is also making solar + BESS more attractive to meet the non-solar hours peaking requirement, competing with new thermal capacities.' This is a competitive-obsolescence risk against the 16,520 MW of coal capacity NTPC currently has under construction.

risks.risk: Daytime solar oversupply compressing market prices and raising price volatility
risks.note: Stated as the threat to the Group's own high-growth RE plans: 'For the high-growth plans of RE capacity addition by NTPC Group, the threat is in form of excess solar supply during day-time compressing market prices and causing high price volatility through the da[y]'. NOTE: this sentence is TRUNCATED mid-word at the end of the MD&A section, so the remainder of management's statement on this risk is not available in the routed text.

risks.risk: Foreign currency exposure on borrowings and procurement contracts
risks.note: Managed through a defined Exchange Risk Management Policy including hedging instruments; during FY 2025-26 the Company entered into derivative contracts aggregating JPY 15,989.65 million, USD 487.66 million and EUR 12.89 million towards management of foreign currency loan exposures. The scale of hedging activity indicates a material FCY-denominated funding base.

risks.risk: Board composition non-compliance - independent directors below the mandated number
risks.note: BACK-FILLED: this risk belongs to the risks domain but appears only in the sibling governance_entities and profile bundles (Corporate Governance Report, section 2.1), not in the risks_esg bundle. Against an approved composition of eight Independent Directors, as on 31 March 2026 the Board had only five; 'During FY 2025-26, numbers of Independent Directors were less than half of the Board' and 'the mandates regarding the presence of a woman independent director and at least 50% non-executive directors were not fulfilled until 18th May 2025'. NTPC has requested the Ministry of Power to make the necessary appointments. A standing SEBI LODR / DPE compliance exposure that the Company cannot itself remedy, since all directors are appointed by the President of India.

one-line thesis: RoE-protected regulated utility compounding on record capacity adds (group >90 GW), where flat revenue masks 18% standalone / 15% group PAT growth because fixed-charge recovery insulates the bottom line from RE-driven thermal backdowns — with embedded optionality in NGEL, BESS, PSP and nuclear.
financial scorecard: One-offs / drivers: Standalone other-expense up 20% (₹5,806→₹6,972 cr) — ₹784 cr ERV (offset by ~₹780 cr regulatory income on sales side, cost-plus pass-through) + ₹478 cr one-time provisions (₹193 cr EESL, ₹149 cr NBPPL, ₹100 cr Garhi Dam). Dividend income from subs/JV ₹2,264 cr (vs ₹2,092 cr). Revenue decline driven by lower daytime PLF (RE injection) — but fixed charges protect margin.
guidance (verify next quarter): Capacity adds (group): FY27 9,557 MW (thermal 1,070 / hydro 250 / RE 8,237); FY28 10,039 MW (thermal 1,460 / hydro 444 / RE 8,135); FY29 11,478 MW (thermal 3,070 / RE 8,408 / no hydro).
RE pace: ~8 GW p.a.; targeting 60 GW by 2032 (aim to beat). FY26 RE plan of ~5 GW slipped partly into FY27.
Group capex: ₹6,22,000 cr to FY32; ~₹3 lakh cr earmarked for RE (NGEL). NGEL capex: FY27 ₹35,800 cr, FY28 ₹46,000 cr, FY29 ₹48,000 cr (80:20 D:E).
Dividend FY26: ₹9/share total (₹5.50 interim + ₹3.50 final proposed).
Next-qtr watch: Patratu Stage-1 Unit-3 commissioning within FY27 (trial of Unit-2 done in Q1 FY27); TTPS Stage-3 / Lara Stage-2 / Sinnar units across FY28-29.
order book & pipeline: Under construction: >34 GW (coal 16.5 GW, hydro ~2.6 GW, RE ~15 GW).
NGEL pipeline: normalized down from 32 GW to 30 GW (actualized contracted+pipeline; MoUs expected to refill).
Coal pipeline: CEA sees 86 GW additional coal need to 2036 (68 GW in pipeline); NTPC executing 16.5 GW + ~4.6 GW in stages.
Transmission tie-up (RE): FY27 firm connectivity 57% + T-GNA 38%; FY28 88% firm + 3% T-GNA (9% open); FY29 84% firm (16% open).
segment / subsidiary detail: NGEL: Generation 14.6 BU (vs 6.8 BU, +114%); FY26 RE add 4,225 MW (vs 2,977 MW FY25); curtailment 314 MUs + TRAS loss 135 MUs; grid-curtailment EBITDA hit ~₹90 cr (TRAS compensated). Subs profit ₹3,312 cr; JV share ₹2,864 cr.

Mining: Captive coal production 47.88 MMT (+8.5%); Pakri Barwadih NW commercial 1-Apr-26; full mining business transferred to NTPC Mining Ltd (BTA complete); captive meets ~18% of coal need; ~18 days coal stock.
Hydro/PSP: TEHRI PSP fully operational (last 250 MW unit COD Apr-26 → 1 GW total).
growth verticals / optionality: BESS: 5 GWh co-located at thermal (cost-plus, CERC tariff framework set); 320 MW standalone (confirmed offtake) + 1,000 MW solar-co-located (tendering) = 1,320 MW on RE side; ~4 GW more planned (Khavda, Bikaner, Fatehgarh, Sitapur, Chhattisgarh); 14.5 GW non-solar connectivity applied with 2-4 hr BESS.
Pumped storage: Group plan ~18,010 MW (NTPC 4,800 + THDC/NEEPCO 13,210); 1 GW already COD; 3-5 GW expected by 2032-33; ~6-7 yr build time.

Nuclear: Mahi Banswara 4x700 MW (2.8 GW) — excavation awarded Sep-25, AERB consent Mar-26, first concrete Aug-27, first synchronization Nov-2032; design consultancy awarded Dec-25; Nuclear Island Mega-EPC NIT by 15-Jun-26, TG Island EPC NIT by 30-Mar-27; 30 sites under study; ASHVINI equity infusion ₹800 cr.
Green fuel: Pudimadaka green-H2 hub (green methanol + SAF); coal gasification pilot at Talaipalli (4 lakh TPA SNG via EIL).
margins & cost dynamics: Cost-plus / regulated RoE model: fixed charges payable once plant is available; technical minimum protected at 55% PLF (below which not obligated to run, still compensated for availability) — SCUC/SCED support up to 55%. Degradation in heat rate/auxiliary consumption within 100-55% band is compensated by regulator.
ERV and O&M increases are largely pass-throughs; bottom-line insulated from low PLF/demand.
WAcost of borrowing fell to 5.98% (FY26) from 6.61% (FY25); $150m JPY (TONA) Mizuho loan at 0.98% over 6M-TONA, 7-yr avg maturity.
capex / expansion: FY26 group capex ₹49,068 cr (vs ₹44,636 cr); standalone ₹28,462 cr (vs ₹22,965 cr).
Long-range ₹6.22 lakh cr to FY32 (~half to RE).
capital allocation: ₹9/share FY26 dividend. GoI raised RE-subsidiary investment limit to ₹20,000 cr (supports 60 GW by 2032 target).
Inorganic RE acquisitions explicitly flagged as a top-up lever.
Possible value-unlock via listing of THDC/NEEPCO/Hindustan Urvarak — "no definitive plans," JV/policy-level decision.
risks & watch-items: RE-driven thermal backdown / falling PLF (regulated structure mitigates, but optics weigh on reported revenue).
Transmission/GNA bottlenecks → curtailment (FY27 only 57% firm connectivity); T-GNA curtailment may rise before tapering.
RE capacity slippage (FY26 5 GW plan spilled into FY27).
Nuclear execution is long-dated (first power 2032) — optionality, not near-term earnings.
One-off provisions (EESL/NBPPL/Garhi Dam) signal subsidiary/receivable risk.
Lower competitive-bid wins in FY26 (NGEL stays away below threshold IRR) — pipeline replenishment dependent on MoUs.
management quality / tone: Confident, granular, disciplined. Multi-year capacity/capex/connectivity/PPA breakdowns volunteered; explicit on RoE-protection mechanics; candid on pipeline normalization (32→30 GW) and bidding discipline. Receivable days improved 29→15. MSCI ESG upgraded CCC→BB. Tone reinforces regulated-compounder narrative.
non-obvious takeaways: Flat top-line is a feature, not a bug: lower PLF cuts both fuel cost and sales while RoE/fixed charges hold — PAT +18% standalone despite revenue -2.69%.
Co-located BESS at thermal plants turns the backdown problem into a peak-discharge revenue stream under cost-plus — a structural hedge against RE cannibalization.
14.5 GW non-solar connectivity application is an under-appreciated round-the-clock/FDRE land grab.
Captive coal at ~18% (rising) materially de-risks fuel cost vs peers reliant on linkage/imports.
NGEL EBITDA margin ~87% with generation +114% — the visible compounder inside the conglomerate.
qoq change log: This quarter (Q4 FY26): Group capacity crossed 90 GW; highest-ever annual add 9,618 MW incl. 1,350 MW Sinnar (MAHAGENCO). PAT +51.4% YoY (Q4) on cost-plus recovery. Pakri Barwadih NW commercial; NTPC Mining BTA complete. TEHRI PSP fully operational. NGEL pipeline normalized 32→30 GW. AERB excavation consent for Mahi Banswara. WAcost of borrowing down to 5.98%. Receivable days 29→15. ₹9/share dividend.

Next-quarter watch items: Patratu Stage-1 Unit-3 commissioning (FY27); Nuclear Island Mega-EPC NIT (15-Jun-26); CUF (solar/wind Q4) and NGEL other-expense breakup promised offline — verify in Q1 FY27 data; RE FY27 connectivity progression from 57%; inorganic RE acquisition announcements; THDC/NEEPCO/Hindustan Urvarak listing clarity.
